name: Zane Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Busy, in a good way. I'm doing environmental science, so I've got lectures on ecosystems and a field trip last week where we measured the pH of a stream and I fell in. Evenings I ride an e-bike delivering food for an app, usually five to ten, more at weekends. I live with my mum in a two-bedroom flat above a dentist. She works part time as a care assistant. I've also got a little side thing where I resell thrifted trainers online.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me how you use AI day to day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Cash flow is the boss. The loan covers fees and not much else. I've got maybe ten days of spending in the bank, since the e-bike needed new brakes last month. Mum can't help, she's stretched. I got in on average grades, so I'm not the star of the course, but I work out stuff fast and I'm not scared of trying things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, I never believed the wildest claims. I'd tell mates it's a good assistant and nothing more. I'd post something like 'it's a tool, not a miracle' and move on. I wouldn't be fussed. It's already useful to me, and that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be mildly disappointed, because part of me likes the idea of something big. But I'm fine, because my plans don't depend on it. I'm more worried about the delivery app cutting rates, which they do anyway. That's the pressure on me, and AI has little to do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: lectures, the bike, the trainer resale. I'd use AI to write the listings and answer customer messages, which saves me an hour a night. I'd try to get some paid fieldwork with the university's environment department, which is more relevant than delivery. I'd also work on stretching my cash to a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easy, a little flat. It's a normal week stretched out over years. I like some change, but I'm fine with this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you lose if it's mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it every day. It drafts my lab reports, then I fix them. It writes my trainer descriptions in thirty seconds. It translates the customers' messages when they write in other languages. If it's all hype, I've still got a daily helper that I'm not paying much for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the real pressure on you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The delivery app changed the pay formula in October and I lost about a fifth of what I make per drop. There's no one to complain to, just a support chatbot. It's got nothing to do with AI hype, it's just a company squeezing riders. I'm looking for something steadier.

Ask the environment department about paid **fieldwork** jobs.
feel: **Easy** and a little flat, like a normal week stretched over years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for people who adapt, and I'd tell my mates to play with it now. I'd be loud about that online, actually. I'd also say companies need to share the gains, because riders and shop staff are going to be the first to get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm nervous about the bike. If customers book and order through AI, the app needs fewer people on the phones. And delivery gets more automated, with robots on pavements in some cities. But I think my science side and my AI skills put me ahead of most of the course. I'm in a decent spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd double down on skills. I'd build a small tool for my side thing, for example one that checks prices on other sites. I'd ask the department about a data analysis module. I'd cut my bike hours slowly as the pay gets worse, and replace them with resale and some freelance work, like tagging data or testing apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired, energised, with a small knot. Like I've found a faster route but there might be a roadblock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your jobs does AI touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The customer chat, the scheduling and the route planning. The app already tells me which restaurant to go to next, and it's getting better. The bike rider part lasts longer than the support part. Walking into a kitchen and asking someone to hurry is hard to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if delivery pay dropped again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the bike to a few peak hours and put the time into freelance work. I'd also keep an eye out for the pickup lockers, since they could cut riders fast. If it goes below what covers my phone bill and bus pass, I'd stop the bike altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, wow, and then I'd say, no one is ready. I'd say it's wild and amazing and terrifying all at once. I'd tell everyone to get stuck in with the tools and not wait. I'd say there should be income support and I'd back whatever party offered it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. I'd act like I'm excited, but I'd be properly scared. My riding job goes sooner than most because the app is basically software already. And I'd only be halfway through my degree. I've got no savings, and Mum's job as a care assistant is also at risk when robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd work out what money I need monthly: rent share, phone, bus pass, food. I'd put every spare pound aside. I'd build something with the AI tools that other people would pay for, a bot for small businesses, say, and pitch it to the cafes I deliver to. I'd keep the degree going, because the environmental side may need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buzzing and sick at the same time. I'd barely sleep but I'd make lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do the week it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots that deliver would come around 2031. So I'd have a few more years of riding after the thinking side changes, which is a small cushion. But the app would cut rates sooner, because it only needs fewer people to run the same system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the three-year gap help a rider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Mum about her job, because care work is hands-on and probably safer for longer, but still. I'd say we need a plan for bills. I'd offer to cover more rent from my side business if it works, and I'd say she shouldn't take on any new debt.

I'd back **income support** from whichever party offers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be huge and we're lucky to see it coming. I'd tell friends to learn to build things with AI, not just use it. And I'd say governments should start now on retraining funds and some form of basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good about it. Five years is enough to finish the degree, build up some skills and a bit of savings. I'd be the guy who knows environmental science and AI, which seems a rare combo. The riding goes first, but the degree is the long-term bet. I'd still worry about my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, use every project to build something with AI, and keep my side business going. I'd stop riding when I can cover rent another way. I'd save a few hundred pounds as a buffer and look for an environmental data internship in my second summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. It's the first one where I can see a path and not just a leap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do five years let you do that two don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me qualify. In two years I'd be a half-finished student with a delivery bike. In five I'd have a degree, a portfolio of AI projects and probably an internship under my belt. That's a different person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the weak point in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cash. I'm good at ideas and bad at saving. If one of my side projects stalls, I've got nothing underneath. So I'd set up an automatic transfer, even twenty pounds a week, where I can't spend it. That's the boring bit I need to learn.

I'd say governments should start retraining funds and **basic income** now.

The degree is my **long-term bet**; riding goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's loads of time and the smart move is to use it. I'd say the schools should be teaching this stuff already. I'd say it's exciting, and I'd probably start a channel on it, because I like explaining things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel pretty good. Ten years means a degree, a master's maybe, a few years of work experience, and a chance to build a proper business. Thinking AI comes by 2036, but I'd already be working with it. The only thing that would sour it is money trouble at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, maybe do a master's in environmental data. I'd work for a firm that uses AI to model climate or water systems. I'd keep a side business. And I'd save, properly this time, for a deposit. I'd also help Mum with a plan for when she retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed. Interested. I'd feel like a guy with a long run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try a couple of different things: a year doing fieldwork, a year in a data job, and see which fits. With a decade, I can afford a couple of detours. I couldn't do that if I only had two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin to learn how things work, not just how to use them. Use the tools every day, but understand what they're doing. And save money early, because it's the one thing that gives you choices.

I'd tell my cousin to **learn how things work**, not just how to use them.

fieldNote: Zane uses time as **room for detours**, which suits his adaptive streak.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything lands before I've got anything in the bank. What would help is cheap, practical courses for people like me, a safety net for gig workers, and rules on delivery apps so they can't change the pay overnight. And honest information from the university about who's hiring.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I think you should ask about the gig bit. A lot of us rely on apps for money, and there's no boss to talk to. If AI changes things, we're the first to feel it and the last to be asked.

headlineQuote: A lot of us rely on apps for money, and there's no boss to talk to.
portrait: Zane is **19**, studying environmental science, riding an e-bike for a delivery app and reselling trainers online.
He is a pragmatic centrist and an **everyday AI user** who moves early on new tools.
His bike income is the **exposed** part; the degree and AI skills are his bet for later.
His mood is anxious in fast worlds and **uneasy** otherwise, because he has no savings.
He turns fear into lists, side projects and pitches to the **cafes** he delivers to.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries him most, because everything lands before he has any savings.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap practical **courses**, a safety net for gig workers and rules on how delivery apps change pay.
